input.question: What was fandom like in ancient Rome for gladiator fights and chariot races?
input.ground_truth: Not exactly Rome, but in very early Byzantium, racing fans where hugely influential in society. By the time of Justinian I, there were two big fanbases: the Greens and the Blues, based on the color of the racers' shirts. There used to be Reds and Whites as well, but they had been absorbed into the other two when the Western Empire fell. However, these where not just sports fans. They had a opinion on, and a say in, many aspects of culture and politics, such as religion, which also divided the two factions. They would often riot and fight, causing literally thousands of deaths. These riots ultimately culminated in the Nika riots, where the two factions united to try and overthrow the Emperor. These riots where huge, costing tens of thousands of lives, and broke the power of the Blues and Greens in street politics, though they continued on in imperial ceremonial roles. Further reading: Alan Cameron, *Circus factions: Blues and Greens at Rome and Byzantium,* Clarendon Press, 1976. _URL_0_

Okay! Imagine a big playground where lots of people come to watch exciting games. In ancient Rome, there was a big place called the Colosseum. People would go there to watch two kinds of fun shows: men fighting with swords (gladiator fights) and fast chariot races, where people rode horses pulling carts and raced really fast.

Now, imagine you really, really like a certain team or a certain gladiator. You want to cheer for them and show everyone you love them! In ancient Rome, people did that too. They would bring banners, shout loudly, and wear special clothes or colors to show which team or fighter they liked. They would cheer and clap and sometimes even throw things to show how excited they were.

So, "fandom" in ancient Rome was like being a super big fan of your favorite sports team or superhero, but instead of football or superheroes, it was gladiators and chariot racers!
